name: Freya Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a senior researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What is your normal workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43, have an MBA and lead seven managers who negotiate service contracts for a large company. I can find a weak promise buried in an appendix and get a supplier to fix it before we sign; colleagues bring me the contracts no one wants to read. I use AI now and then to compare two versions after another buyer has tested it, then read the source pages myself. I like a repair crew arriving when promised and hate a cheap clause that strands a site.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is going on at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works restaurant hours that swing with the season, and we have two children at school and a mortgage. My salary is low for this level despite years of strong results, and there is less than a month of expenses saved with few similar manager posts nearby. I can negotiate a contract; I cannot negotiate the bank balance at the end of a quiet week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our contracts group that an AI comparison of old and new service terms can save time, as long as someone checks what the supplier really promised. A cheaper clause is useless if the repair crew cannot reach a site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lead seven contract managers and have an MBA; negotiating a broken service promise is the part of the job I do well. My pay sits below other managers here, my partner's restaurant hours change by season, and with two children, a mortgage and less than a month saved, a quiet year is still financially loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On Thursday I'll keep the contract review meeting and use AI only for a draft comparison of two maintenance agreements after checking the source pages. In the first year of the plateau, I'll ask for a pay regrade with the three contracts where my team recovered missed service, then put any actual raise into cash after the mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the bank balance, not the small AI comparison. Some months my partner's rota cuts the margin we thought we had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What was missed in one of those contracts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A repair supplier wrote 'next working day' on the front page, while an appendix allowed three days for remote sites. I found it before we signed and made the firm put the same promise on both pages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not save before getting a raise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We already save what survives the mortgage and the children's meals, and some months that is nothing. I won't write a number into a budget that depends on restaurant hours we haven't seen.

say: I'd use **draft clause comparisons** only after checking the supplier's source pages.
I'd say a **cheap promise** means little if the repair crew cannot arrive.
think: My **negotiation skill** is strong, but low manager pay and seasonal restaurant work keep our cash thin.
A quiet AI year does not solve the **mortgage margin** at home.
do: Keep **Thursday contract reviews** and check AI comparisons against source pages.
Seek a **pay regrade** using three recovered-service contracts; save any actual raise after mortgage and school costs.
feel: She feels **anxious** about household cash, while minor AI changes seem manageable.
S0.quote: A cheaper clause is useless if the repair crew cannot reach a site.
fieldNote: Her **senior negotiating skill** coexists with lower pay, variable partner hours and under-one-month savings.
The three-day appendix gives a **concrete reason** for checking an AI clause comparison.

steps.text: Keep Thursday contract review and verify AI comparisons against signed source pages
Save any actual pay regrade after mortgage and school costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the contract managers Steady Disruption will automate drafting, price checks and supplier questions, and our company must put retraining and staffing numbers in writing. I'd support a trial on expired agreements before it touches live service promises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can negotiate well, but if software prepares nearly every clause, one senior manager might cover two teams and mine could be combined. My partner's seasonal hours would not carry the mortgage alone, and there are few comparable posts near our children's school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I'll ask the workers' council for a joint trial on ten expired service agreements, with supplier errors visible to the team. In the first year of disruption, if the trial meets our service standard and the company gives paid training with a real instructor, I'd learn the clause tool myself; if my post is merged, I'd check a nearby procurement lead vacancy only if its wage covers mortgage and child care, keeping my present job until a written offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a smaller management layer. I am willing to learn a proven tool, but not to sign a live contract with an untested promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the trial fail?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the tool misses a three-day exception and labels it next-day service, we stop. A site manager cannot plan a repair around a promise that exists only in a summary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell the council about your own risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I'd also show how the team's check saved the company a bad contract. The staffing discussion should include those people, not treat an empty chair as a saving.

say: I'd ask for **written staffing and training** as drafting and checking move to software.
I'd support a **trial on expired agreements** before live service promises change.
think: My skill may not prevent **two management teams** from being combined.
Seasonal partner income and few local posts make our **mortgage vulnerable** to my lost wage.
do: Ask the **workers' council** for a ten-agreement trial with visible supplier errors.
Learn the **clause tool** only after a sound trial with paid learning time and a real instructor.
If merged, seek **procurement work** only with mortgage-and-childcare pay; keep current job until written offer.
feel: She feels **anxious** about a merged post while open to a proven tool.
S1.quote: A site manager cannot plan a repair around a promise that exists only in a summary.
fieldNote: She tests **service exceptions** rather than generic draft speed, using the appendix error she already knows.
Her personal learning depends on **paid instruction**, and any job move requires mortgage and child-care pay.

steps.text: Bring ten expired service agreements to workers council for joint trial
Learn clause tool only if trial meets standard and company funds paid time with instructor
Apply for procurement lead after merger if pay covers mortgage and childcare; stay until written offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team AGI by 2028 can prepare and compare almost any service contract, so the company needs to state which people still sign and answer for a failed promise. I'd ask for the staffing date and the rule for challenging a bad automated clause.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The negotiating plan and clause judgment are thinking work that AGI reaches in 2028; robots around 2031 may repair sites later, but that does not delay my desk. I think the company could remove my post, and under a month of cash would not cover the mortgage while I hunted for a rare local manager role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I'll ask HR for written severance terms and take our mortgage and school bills to the kitchen table with my partner. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2028, if I still lead contracts, I'd check its service clauses against signed supplier promises; if cut, I'd apply for procurement roles outside this town only where posted pay covers the mortgage, child care and travel, and accept only a written offer before giving notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed; this is the quick one where the school payment and mortgage both arrive before a new salary. I can negotiate a price, but I cannot negotiate another month into our savings account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take contract work while searching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only with a signed fee and payment date before the mortgage falls due. A supplier can promise an interesting project. My family cannot eat an interesting project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your team if your own post goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the date the company gave me and what I know about appeals, not pretend our contracts are safe because we have good judgment. I would ask the council to check that each person gets the same written terms.

say: I'd demand **staffing dates** and a person answerable for bad AGI clauses.
I'd tell colleagues **contract judgment** changes in 2028, before site robots arrive.
think: My **senior desk role** faces 2028 AGI; 2031 repair robots offer no delay.
Under one month saved makes a lost wage a fast **mortgage and school-cost threat**.
do: Seek **written severance terms** now and review mortgage and school bills with my partner.
After 2028, check **AGI clauses** if employed; apply outside town only for posted pay covering mortgage, care and travel.
Accept only a **written offer** before giving notice; take projects only with signed fee paid before mortgage.
feel: She feels **alarmed** by the short time between losing pay and the next family bills.
S2.quote: My family cannot eat an interesting project.
fieldNote: Her **high skill** cannot cover a mortgage without wages when AGI reaches contract thinking in 2028.
Outside work requires **viable pay** and travel, while contract projects need signed fees before bills are due.

steps.text: Check AGI service clauses against signed promises after 2028 if employed
Apply outside town only if posted pay covers mortgage, childcare and travel after cut
Accept outside role only after written offer confirms mortgage, childcare and travel pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2031 gives us five years to make supplier disputes transparent and give contract staff a real place in the decision. I'd ask the workers' council to bargain for funded training before any team is cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years might let us save a few months if my partner's restaurant shifts steady, and I could gain more experience settling delivery failures face to face. But AGI can reason through disputes in 2031 too; robots around 2034 might later do physical repair, not shield my contracting job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From next spring, I'd take a short supplier-dispute course only if the company funds both fee and paid hours, and practise two live calls with our service lead. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, I'd seek a retained dispute manager post only if it actually exists at pay covering mortgage and child care; otherwise I'd apply to nearby buyer offices without leaving my current wage until a written offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but five years gives us room to ask better questions and make a cash plan. I would not promise the children a new job based on a course badge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would you save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If restaurant shifts are booked for three months ahead, we'd put an extra 120 monthly into cash after the mortgage. If the rota keeps changing, I won't call the transfer a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why learn disputes if AGI can do them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A supplier still has a person across the table today, and I want to improve how I handle that conversation. I know the post itself may go in 2031; the practice isn't a guarantee.

say: I'd seek **funded dispute training** and council input before contract teams are cut.
I'd ask for **transparent supplier decisions** as 2031 approaches.
think: Booked restaurant shifts might let us build a **larger reserve** before 2031.
Supplier dispute judgment is **thinking work** exposed in 2031; later robots offer no desk delay.
do: Take **supplier-dispute training** only if company funds fee and paid hours, with two live calls.
Save **120 monthly** after mortgage only with three months of booked shifts; seek retained dispute post with viable pay.
If none exists, check **nearby buyer offices** while employed until a written offer.
feel: She feels **anxious** despite five years because the household cash plan depends on booked shifts.
S3.quote: I would not promise the children a new job based on a course badge.
fieldNote: The course is **funded and practised live**, not an assumed safety route from AGI.
Her saving target needs **three booked months** of restaurant shifts after the mortgage, not hope alone.

steps.text: Take supplier-dispute course only if company funds fee and paid time with two live calls
Save extra 120 monthly after mortgage if restaurant shifts booked three months ahead
Apply for retained dispute post after 2031 only if vacancy pays mortgage and childcare
Apply nearby if no retained dispute post, keeping wage until written offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the contract team AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to build fair transition rules while we are still paid to work. I would ask the workers' council to publish how many people actually moved into paid posts each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 in 2036 and our children will be older, but I won't assume the mortgage is finished. I could use the decade to become better at resolving supplier failures; that is still thinking work AGI could do in 2036, and robots around 2039 only affect the physical repair side later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll keep reviewing major service agreements and bring one supplier failure each quarter to the council's transition meeting. I'd ask for a pay regrade again and set aside any actual rise after the mortgage; in the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, I'd stay only in a paid role with authority over real supplier outcomes, otherwise seek an actual vacancy at another firm while keeping my wage until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel watchful rather than reassured by a decade. I know how to plan a contract, but the restaurant rota can still erase our spare cash next week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you push your children toward a different career?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd tell them to learn what they care about, then ask how a job is paid and who can change a bad decision. I won't use their school choices to solve my pay problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What authority would make you stay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd need to change a supplier's service plan when a site is stranded, not just approve a screen's recommendation. A manager title with no power to fix the site is only a signature on a missed repair.

say: I'd seek **annual paid-move counts** and fair transition rules through the council.
I'd say a decade lets us build **fair transition rules** while we are still paid to work.
think: At **53**, our children will be older but the mortgage may remain.
Supplier outcomes still involve **thinking work** exposed in 2036; 2039 robots add no desk delay.
do: Keep **major agreement reviews** and bring quarterly failures to the council this year.
Request a **pay regrade** and save any actual rise after mortgage.
After 2036, stay for **paid supplier authority**; otherwise seek actual vacancies while keeping wage until signed offer.
feel: She feels **watchful**, with ten years to plan but variable restaurant income now.
S4.quote: A manager title with no power to fix the site is only a signature on a missed repair.
fieldNote: Her senior expertise gives her **bargaining evidence**, but the thin cushion still shapes the mood.
She measures a long transition by **paid moves and authority**, while acknowledging dispute work remains exposed.

steps.text: Keep reviewing major service agreements this year
Bring one supplier failure quarterly to workers council transition meeting
Save any actual pay regrade after mortgage payment
Seek actual vacancy after 2036 if no paid supplier authority, keeping wage until signed offer

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because contract reasoning could be bought cheaply before our household has cash to cover a lost salary. Written staffing and severance dates, funded practice on live supplier disputes and a real vacancy with enough pay would help us protect the mortgage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the stranded site manager whether a cheap service clause delivered a repair. A supplier promise belongs in the driveway, not only in an appendix.

headlineQuote: A supplier promise belongs in the driveway, not only in an appendix.
portrait: At **43**, Freya is an MBA-trained senior service-contract manager who catches weak clauses and sometimes uses checked AI comparisons.
Her **low pay**, seasonal partner hours, mortgage and under-one-month cushion keep money tense even in a plateau.
She asks the **workers' council** for trials and paid training while protecting live supplier promises.
Fast AGI threatens **contract reasoning**; longer runways offer practice, though supplier disputes remain thinking-exposed.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her skilled contract wage before savings cover the mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: **Written staffing terms**, funded live practice and a viable vacancy would help the household plan.
